title: Headworks of run-of-river (ROR) plants
summary: This is the subchapter most specific to Nepal, because run-of-river schemes dominate the country and their headworks must cope with steep, boulder-laden mountain streams. The sequence matters and is examined: trench weir or side intake, then gravel trap, then settling basin, each removing a coarser fraction than the next. Understand why the settling basin targets 0.2 to 0.3 mm and why abrasive Himalayan quartz destroys turbine runners, because that single fact justifies most of the expenditure at the headworks.

sections.heading: The problem and the sequence
sections.body:
**What a run-of-river headworks must do**, in a Himalayan setting:

| Requirement | Difficulty |
|---|---|
| **Divert the design flow reliably**, including in the dry season | Low flows are small and the channel shifts |
| **Exclude BOULDERS and coarse bedload** | Mountain streams roll large stones in flood |
| **Exclude floating debris** | Logs, branches, plastic |
| **Remove abrasive SEDIMENT** before the turbine | Himalayan quartz destroys runners |
| **Pass the design flood** without damage | Flash floods, debris flows |
| **Release the environmental flow** continuously | A legal requirement |
| Survive with minimal operation | Remote sites, limited staff |

**The sequence of structures**, and each removes a **coarser fraction than the next** — which is the organising logic and a standard examination question:

> **Diversion weir and INTAKE → GRAVEL TRAP → SETTLING (desilting) BASIN → headrace**

| Structure | Removes | Size range |
|---|---|---|
| **Trash rack at the intake** | Floating debris, logs | Large objects |
| **Intake sill / bed load exclusion** | Rolling **boulders and cobbles** | Above ~50 mm |
| **GRAVEL TRAP** | **Coarse bedload** | Above about **2 mm** |
| **SETTLING BASIN** | **Suspended sediment** | Above about **0.2 – 0.3 mm** |
| (Turbine tolerates the remainder) | Fine silt and clay | Below 0.2 mm |

**Skipping the gravel trap chokes the settling basin within a single monsoon**, which is why the sequence cannot be compressed. A settling basin is designed to trap particles by **slow sedimentation over a long surface**; feeding it gravel fills its storage volume immediately and leaves it no capacity for the fine material it exists to catch.

Equally, **feeding gravel into the headrace** abrades a canal lining or a tunnel invert and deposits in the forebay.

**Why sediment removal matters so much — the justification for the expenditure:**

| Factor | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Himalayan sediment is **abundant** | Very high concentrations in monsoon flood |
| It is **quartz-rich and therefore HARD** | Harder than the steel of a runner |
| It is **angular** | Cuts rather than polishes |
| Turbine velocities are **high** | Erosion rate rises steeply with velocity |

> Together these can **destroy a turbine runner within a single monsoon season** if the settling basin is inadequate.

The damage takes the form of **abrasive erosion** of Pelton buckets and needles, and of Francis runner blades, guide vanes and labyrinth seals. The consequences are **loss of efficiency** (progressive, and often unnoticed until output is measurably down), **vibration and cavitation** (as the profile is spoilt), and eventually **replacement of the runner** — a major cost and a long outage.

The particles that do the damage are the **hard fraction above roughly 0.2 mm**, which is exactly why the settling basin's target size is set there. Removing finer material would require an impractically large basin for little benefit; leaving coarser material would destroy the machine.

sections.heading: Intake types
sections.body:
**The choice of intake is governed by the river's character**, and Nepal spans several:

| Intake | Character | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Side intake** | An opening in the bank behind a diversion weir, with a raised sill | **Larger rivers**, moderate slope, stable channel |
| **Trench weir (Tyrolean / bottom rack) intake** | A **trench across the bed** covered by a **coarse screen**, through which water falls | **Steep, boulder-laden mountain streams** — the Nepali standard for small and medium schemes |
| Frontal / bottom intake | Water drawn from the bed directly | Small streams |
| Infiltration gallery | A perforated pipe buried in the permeable bed | Very high sediment; small flows |
| Reservoir / canal intake | — | Storage schemes, canal-based |

**The trench weir (Tyrolean) intake deserves full explanation**, because it is the characteristic Nepali solution and its cleverness lies in what it does *not* try to do:

**How it works.** A **trench** is built across the stream bed, covered by a **screen (rack) of steel bars** inclined slightly downstream, with the bars running **parallel to the flow**. Water falls **through** the screen into the trench and is conveyed away; **boulders, cobbles and debris pass OVER** the screen and continue down the river.

**Why it suits Himalayan streams:**

| Advantage | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Bedload passes over** rather than into the intake | No boulder enters the waterway |
| **No high weir to be destroyed** by a flood or debris flow | The structure is low and within the bed |
| **Works at very low flow** | Even a shallow flow falls through the rack |
| **Little operation required** | No gates to set |
| **Debris self-clears** | The flow sweeps it over |

**Its design points:**

| Point | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Bar spacing** | Set by the gravel trap's tolerance — typically **20–50 mm clear** |
| **Bar orientation** | **Parallel to the flow**, so stones roll over rather than jamming across |
| **Rack inclination** | About **10–20°** downstream, aiding self-clearing |
| **Rack area** | Generous, since part will always be blocked |
| **Trench slope and velocity** | Self-cleansing, so the trench does not silt |
| Flushing arrangement | To scour accumulated material from the trench |

**Its limitation** is that the rack can be **blinded by fine debris, leaves or ice**, and in very large flows it may draw in more sediment than a side intake would. Regular **raking** remains necessary despite the self-clearing tendency.

**The side intake** is the conventional alternative, and its design points are those of any canal head regulator:

| Point | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Sill raised above the river bed** | So the intake **skims the cleaner upper layer** and bedload passes beneath |
| **Located on the CONCAVE (outer) bank of a bend** where possible | The **helical current** carries bedload toward the convex bank, so the outer bank offers **deeper, cleaner water** |
| **Approach angle** oblique to the flow | Reduces sediment entry |
| **Trash rack** and **gates** | Debris exclusion and flow control |
| **Under-sluice / flushing sluice** adjacent | Scours the accumulated deposit in front of the intake |
| **Divide wall** | Creates a still pocket for settling |

**The concave-bank siting is a free advantage from the river's own hydraulics**, and it is worth stating why: in a bend, the water surface superelevates outward, driving a **secondary current** that flows outward at the surface and **inward along the bed**. The bed load is therefore swept **toward the inner (convex) bank**, where a point bar forms, while the outer bank is **scoured and deep**. An intake there gets depth and relatively clean water without any structure to achieve it.

**Diversion weir.** For a run-of-river scheme the weir is usually **low** — it need only raise the level enough to feed the intake, not to store — and is often a simple **concrete or gabion structure**. Its design must nevertheless address:

| Consideration | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Design flood passage** | Without damage or excessive afflux |
| **Scour** downstream | Apron, cut-off, launching apron |
| **Seepage and uplift** | As for any weir on permeable foundation (Khosla) |
| **Energy dissipation** | Cistern or stone protection |
| **Environmental release** | A notch, orifice or pipe passing the mandatory flow continuously |
| **Fish passage** | Where migratory species are present |

**The environmental release arrangement** deserves note: it must be **passive and continuously effective**, not dependent on an operator opening a valve. A **fixed notch or orifice at the weir**, sized to pass the required flow at the normal pond level, is the usual and correct solution — because a release that depends on operation is a release that will stop.

sections.heading: Gravel trap and settling basin
sections.body:
**The gravel trap** is a short, deepened section immediately after the intake, in which the **velocity is reduced enough for coarse material to drop out**.

| Feature | Typical |
|---|---|
| **Target particle size** | Above about **2 mm** |
| **Velocity** | Reduced to about **0.6 – 1.0 m/s** |
| **Length** | Short — a few metres |
| **Depth** | A trap depth of 0.5 – 1.0 m below the invert |
| **Flushing** | A **flushing gate** discharging back to the river, operated frequently in the monsoon |

Its flushing arrangement is essential and must have **adequate head and slope** to carry the gravel back to the river — a flushing pipe that cannot move a 20 mm stone is useless. Because it fills quickly in flood, it is flushed **daily or more often** during the monsoon, which is one of the few routine operating tasks at a remote headworks.

**The settling (desilting) basin** removes the **suspended** fraction, and its design is the same ideal-settling theory as a water treatment sedimentation tank.

**The design principle:**

> A particle is removed if its **settling velocity v_s exceeds Q/A_surface**

so — as in water treatment — the **efficiency depends on the SURFACE AREA, not the depth**. To improve a basin, increase its plan area (or add plate settlers), not its depth.

**Design values:**

| Parameter | Typical |
|---|---|
| **Target particle size** | **0.2 – 0.3 mm** (sometimes 0.15 mm where the sediment is especially hard) |
| **Settling velocity for 0.2 mm sand** | About **0.02 m/s** (Stokes/Rubey) |
| **Through velocity** | **0.2 – 0.5 m/s** — low enough to settle, high enough not to deposit the fines that should pass |
| **Length** | From the settling time and the through velocity; commonly 30–80 m |
| Depth | 2 – 4 m, plus storage for the deposit |
| **Trapping efficiency** | Designed for 80–95% of the target size and above |
| **Inlet transition** | **Gradual**, to distribute the flow uniformly across the width |

**The inlet transition is the detail that decides whether the basin works.** A basin fed by an abrupt expansion develops a **jet down the centre and eddies at the sides**, so most of the water passes through in a fraction of the nominal detention time and settles nothing. A **long gradual transition, with baffles or a diffuser wall**, distributes the flow across the full width — which is what the surface-area theory assumes. Short-circuiting is the commonest reason a basin underperforms its design.

**Types of settling basin:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Intermittent (batch) flushing** | Fills with deposit, then the plant is **shut down or switched to a second bay** while the basin is flushed. Simple but interrupts generation |
| **Continuous flushing** | A **hopper bottom with a continuous flushing duct** removes the deposit while the basin remains in service — no interruption, but it **continuously spends water** |
| **Two-bay (duplicate)** | One bay operates while the other is flushed — the usual solution for a plant that must not stop |

**The trade-off is between water and continuity**, and it is a real design decision: continuous flushing spends perhaps **5–10% of the diverted flow** on flushing, which is energy foregone; intermittent flushing spends less water but stops generation. A **two-bay basin** costs more in civil works and resolves both, which is why it is standard on medium and large schemes.

**Flushing requirements:** an adequate **head difference** to the river, a **steep flushing duct** with self-cleansing velocity, and a **flushing outlet** located so the discharged sediment does not simply deposit at the intake again — a mistake that has been made.

**Sediment sampling and design** is where this connects to the investigation stage. The basin's target size follows from the **turbine type and head**, and the **quantity of deposit** to be stored follows from the **measured concentration and gradation** of the river's sediment. A basin designed on an assumed concentration, without measurement, is a guess — and since the consequence of getting it wrong is a destroyed runner, it is a guess with an expensive downside.

**Recommended target sizes by machine**, as a guide:

| Turbine | Target removal |
|---|---|
| **High-head Pelton** | **0.1 – 0.2 mm** — most sensitive, because jet velocities are highest |
| Francis | 0.2 – 0.3 mm |
| Kaplan (low head) | 0.3 – 0.5 mm — least sensitive |

**The high-head Pelton is the most vulnerable**, which is counter-intuitive until the reason is seen: the **jet velocity in a Pelton is proportional to √H**, so a 400 m head gives a jet of nearly 90 m/s, and abrasive wear rises steeply — roughly with the **third power** of velocity. That is why high-head Nepali schemes invest most heavily in desilting.

sections.heading: Forebay, surge tank and the transition to the penstock
sections.body:
**The forebay** sits at the end of a **free-surface headrace (canal)**, at the head of the penstock.

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Short-term storage (pondage)** | Absorbs **load fluctuation** — when the turbine demand rises, the forebay supplies immediately while the canal accelerates |
| **Final settling opportunity** | A last chance for any remaining sediment to drop out |
| **Ensures SUBMERGENCE** | So **no air is drawn into the penstock** |
| **Spillway** | Discharges surplus when the turbine load falls, preventing the canal overtopping |
| **Trash rack** and gate | Final debris exclusion; isolation of the penstock |
| Flushing outlet | Removes deposited sediment |

**The submergence requirement is the one candidates overlook.** If the water level over the penstock intake is insufficient, a **vortex forms and draws air down the penstock**. Air in a penstock is seriously damaging: it causes **water hammer on collapse**, **loss of discharge**, **vibration**, and — if it reaches the turbine — **loss of output and damage**. The minimum submergence is therefore specified from empirical criteria (commonly a multiple of the intake diameter, with a **vortex-suppressing** arrangement such as a floor or wall close to the intake).

**The forebay's spillway is equally essential and equally easy to omit.** When the turbine load drops suddenly, the penstock demand falls to nearly zero while the **canal continues to deliver** its full flow for the minutes it takes to close the intake gate. Without a spillway, the forebay overtops — and an overtopping forebay on a steep hillside starts a landslide. The spillway must therefore be sized for the **full canal discharge**.

**The surge tank** performs the analogous role for a **pressure conduit (tunnel)** rather than a free-surface canal.

> A **surge tank** is provided on a **LONG pressure conduit** to absorb **water hammer** and to **supply water on load acceptance**.

**Why it is needed.** In a long pressure tunnel, a **sudden change in turbine discharge** cannot be accommodated by the water column, which has enormous inertia. Closing the turbine sends a **pressure wave** back up the conduit; opening it demands water the conduit cannot accelerate instantly. A surge tank, open to the atmosphere, provides a **free water surface close to the turbine**:

| On load rejection (closure) | On load acceptance (opening) |
|---|---|
| The **water rises** in the surge tank, absorbing the surge | The **surge tank supplies water immediately** while the long conduit accelerates |
| Converts a **pressure wave problem** into a **mass oscillation** problem | Prevents a pressure drop and possible separation |

**Converting a pressure wave into a mass oscillation is the essential idea**: a pressure wave travels at about **1440 m/s** and produces very high pressures, whereas a mass oscillation is a slow rise and fall of a water surface, easily accommodated by making the tank tall enough. The surge tank does not eliminate the surge; it **changes its character to one that can be contained**.

**Is a surge tank needed?** The usual criterion compares the **conduit length to the head**:

> A surge tank is generally required when **L/H exceeds about 5**, or when the **water hammer pressure rise would be unacceptable**

so a **short penstock does not need one** — which is why many small Nepali schemes with a canal headrace and a short penstock have a forebay and no surge tank at all.

**Types of surge tank:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Simple** | A plain vertical shaft; large oscillations, slowly damped |
| **Restricted orifice (throttled)** | A **throttle** at the base **damps the oscillation quickly** by dissipating energy, so a smaller tank suffices — but it transmits a higher initial pressure to the tunnel |
| **Differential (Johnson)** | An inner riser plus an outer tank; **rapid initial response** from the riser with the damping of a large tank |
| **Expansion chamber** | Chambers at the top and bottom to limit the extreme levels in a confined shaft |
| Air cushion surge chamber | A sealed chamber with compressed air; used where a shaft to the surface is impractical |

**The differential surge tank** is the most refined and its logic is elegant: the **narrow inner riser responds immediately** to a change in discharge (giving prompt regulation, which the governor needs), while the **large outer tank provides the volume** to absorb the surge and damp the oscillation. It obtains both quick response and effective damping, which a simple tank cannot.

**Air cushion surge chambers** are worth knowing as the modern alternative for deep underground schemes: instead of a shaft rising to the surface — which in a mountain may be hundreds of metres of expensive excavation — a **sealed chamber part-filled with compressed air** provides the same compliance. It has been used in Norway extensively and is applicable to Nepal's underground schemes.

**The transition to the penstock** — the last elements of the headworks:

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **Trash rack** | Final debris exclusion; bar spacing set by the turbine |
| **Intake (penstock) gate** | Isolation for maintenance; emergency closure |
| **Air vent / air valve** | **Admits air when the penstock is drained** (preventing collapse under vacuum) and releases it on filling |
| **Bellmouth entry** | Reduces entry loss and vortex formation |
| Bypass and filling valve | Controlled filling of the penstock |

**The air vent is a safety-critical item.** A penstock being **drained** with its air vent blocked or absent develops an internal **vacuum**, and a thin-walled steel penstock will **collapse inward** under external atmospheric pressure — a failure mode requiring no water pressure at all. Penstocks have been lost this way, and it is why the vent is sized for the drainage rate and its outlet kept clear.

formulas.label: The headworks sequence
formulas.expression: intake (trench weir or side) → GRAVEL TRAP (> 2 mm) → SETTLING BASIN (> 0.2–0.3 mm) → headrace
formulas.note: Each stage removes a coarser fraction than the next. Skipping the gravel trap chokes the basin in one monsoon.

formulas.label: Settling basin design principle
formulas.expression: A particle is removed if its settling velocity exceeds Q/A_surface
formulas.note: Efficiency depends on SURFACE AREA, not depth. Short-circuiting from a poor inlet transition is the usual failure.

formulas.label: Settling basin design values
formulas.expression: target 0.2–0.3 mm ; through velocity 0.2–0.5 m/s ; settling velocity for 0.2 mm sand ≈ 0.02 m/s
formulas.note: Continuous flushing spends 5–10% of the diverted flow; a two-bay basin avoids both interruption and that loss.

formulas.label: Target removal size by turbine
formulas.expression: high-head Pelton 0.1–0.2 mm ; Francis 0.2–0.3 mm ; Kaplan 0.3–0.5 mm
formulas.note: Pelton is most sensitive because jet velocity ∝ √H and wear rises roughly with the cube of velocity.

formulas.label: Gravel trap
formulas.expression: target > 2 mm ; velocity reduced to 0.6–1.0 m/s ; flushed daily or more often in the monsoon
formulas.note: The flushing arrangement needs enough head and slope to actually move gravel back to the river.

formulas.label: Trench weir (Tyrolean) intake
formulas.expression: Bars PARALLEL to the flow, inclined ~10–20° downstream, clear spacing 20–50 mm
formulas.note: Water falls through; boulders and debris pass OVER. The Nepali standard for steep boulder streams.

formulas.label: Surge tank requirement
formulas.expression: Generally required when L/H exceeds about 5, or when the water hammer rise is unacceptable
formulas.note: It converts a pressure WAVE problem (c ≈ 1440 m/s) into a slow MASS OSCILLATION that can be contained.

formulas.label: Forebay spillway capacity
formulas.expression: Sized for the FULL canal discharge
formulas.note: On sudden load rejection the canal keeps delivering while the penstock demand falls to zero.
